topics.title: How does a car engine actually work?

cards.title: Tiny controlled explosions, one after another.
cards.text: Fuel and air are trapped in a tube, the cylinder, and lit. The very hot gas pushes hard on a sliding plug, the piston. A wheel needs spin, not a push.

cards.title: A bent shaft turns the shove into a spin
cards.text: A rod links the piston to a bent shaft, the crankshaft. Pushing the bend turns it, like a foot on a bike pedal. What brings the piston back up?

cards.title: One bang takes four strokes, two full turns
cards.text: Each trip up or down is a stroke: suck in, squeeze, bang, blow out. Four half-turns make two turns. Only the bang pushes; the shaft's spin carries the piston through the rest.

cards.title: Why squeeze the fuel before lighting it?
cards.text: Squeezing first packs the fuel and air tight and warm. After the burn, that gas is under far more pressure, so the bang hits like a punch, not a nudge.

cards.title: So engines use several cylinders, taking turns
cards.text: One cylinder bangs once per two turns, so the engine shudders. Four share those two turns, one bang every half turn, and feel smooth. Tap 4.

cards.note: The spin still has to reach the wheels, and a steep hill makes that hard.

topics.title: Why does a slower gear make a steep hill easier?

cards.title: Same hill, same legs, different gear.
cards.text: Shifting gear changes how your pedals drive the wheel. In one gear you stand on the pedals and barely move. In another, the same hill is easy.

steps.note: Other gear: light push, keeps climbing

cards.title: A longer spanner turns a stuck bolt
cards.text: Turning force is how hard the bolt gets twisted. Push twice as far out, get twice the twist. The price: your hand travels further for the same turn.

cards.title: One big-gear turn costs 3 small-gear turns
cards.text: Gears are wheels with teeth. The small gear's teeth push the big gear round, like a spanner on a bolt. 36 teeth to 12 means 3 small turns per big one.

visual.tip: Drag the gear to turn it

cards.title: The big gear is a spanner 3 times longer
cards.text: The teeth meet at each gear's edge with the same push. The big gear's edge is 3 times as far from its middle as the small one's: 3 times the turning force.

cards.title: That is your bike's easy gear on the hill
cards.text: A chain links the small front gear you pedal to the big back one. Say 3 pedal turns give 1 wheel turn, each push worth 3. A hill needs force, not speed.

cards.title: A car needs its easy gear to start
cards.text: A stopped car is heavy to get rolling, so it starts in an easy pair of gears. Cruising uses faster pairs. A gearbox holds them all.
cards.takeaway: Gears trade speed for turning force.

topics.title: Why does ice float on the very water it came from?

cards.text: Most solids sink in their own melted liquid. Ice is the odd one out: a cube bobs on its own water, mostly hidden below. What did freezing change?

steps.note: The stone sinks. The ice floats.
Most of the ice sits underwater

cards.title: Frozen water locks into roomy rings
cards.text: Water is made of tiny pieces that slide past each other. Freeze it and they lock into six-sided rings. The gaps are extra room, so ice takes up more space.

steps.note: Ice: locked in rings, with gaps

cards.title: The same water takes more room as ice
cards.text: A full bottle cracks when frozen: ice takes about a tenth more room. So a glass of ice weighs less than a glass of water, and the heavier water holds it up.

steps.note: A bottle filled to the top

cards.note: Because ice floats, lakes freeze from the top down. The water underneath stays liquid, so fish can survive the winter.

topics.title: Why is the sky blue, but red at sunset?

cards.title: The same sun paints two different skies.
cards.text: Sunlight is every colour mixed together. So something in the air must be sorting them.

cards.title: Air scatters blue light far more than red
cards.text: Light travels in waves: blue short and tightly packed, red long and lazy. The shorter the wave, the more tiny gas specks scatter it in new directions.

cards.title: Scattered blue reaches you from everywhere
cards.text: Scattered blue flies off in every direction, so some always reaches your eyes, wherever you look.
cards.takeaway: That is the blue sky. So why red at sunset?

cards.title: At sunset, light crosses far more air
cards.text: Air wraps round Earth like a skin. A low sun shines sideways through far more of it, flinging blue away and leaving red and orange to reach you.

steps.note: Noon: a short trip through air
Blue flung off, red gets through

cards.note: Violet scatters even more, but the sun gives off less of it and our eyes notice it less, so we see blue.

topics.title: How does your phone know exactly where you are?

cards.title: It never calls a satellite. It just listens.
cards.text: Satellites keep broadcasting two things: where they are, and the exact time they sent the signal. Your phone only listens, then works out where it is.

cards.title: A storm shows how a delay becomes distance
cards.text: Lightning and thunder start together, but light arrives at once and sound crawls. Every 3 seconds between flash and boom is about 1 km. GPS also turns a delay into a distance.

steps.note: The flash reaches you at once
The boom is slow, so it is late

cards.title: A satellite signal is a very fast thunderclap
cards.text: Each signal has the time it was sent. A signal moves at the speed of light. From straight above (20,200 kilometers), it takes about 0.07 seconds. Your phone measures this time. The time gives the distance.

cards.title: One distance gives a ring of places
cards.text: Look at a map from above. You are on the ground. The satellite is a known distance away. You can be at any place that is this far from the satellite. These places make a ring.

cards.title: More satellites give one place
cards.text: Two satellites give two rings. The rings cross at two places. A third ring usually goes through only one of them.

steps.note: Two rings cross in two spots
Only one spot fits all three

cards.note: Timing must be exact: a thousandth of a second off is a 300 km mistake. Phone clocks are cheap, so a fourth satellite helps: four signals together solve your 3D position and the clock error.

topics.title: What happens in the two seconds after you tap your card?

cards.title: Message first. The shop's money later.
cards.text: The tap sends a short message toward your bank, through the shop's bank and a card network. Your bank answers yes or no, and the answer hops back.

steps.note: A message hops to your bank

cards.title: Why does the message detour through a network?
cards.text: Without one, each shop's bank would need a link to every customer's bank, thousands in all. Card networks like Visa connect the banks that belong to them, so a tap reaches yours.

steps.note: Every pair needs its own link

cards.title: How does your bank decide so fast?
cards.text: A computer checks the card is real and you can pay. If yes, it holds that amount, so you cannot spend it twice. The shop is not paid yet.

steps.note: The shop is not paid yet

cards.title: So when does the shop actually get paid?
cards.text: Paying tap by tap would be slow and costly. So banks batch payments, like counting the till at closing time.
cards.takeaway: The shop is paid in one to a few working days.

steps.note: Tap, then yes, in about 2 sec
Payments are added up in batches

cards.note: Another thing that feels instant but takes a trip: your phone finding where you are.
